extracted.intended_audience: Korean policymakers, central administrative agencies, and regulatory reform practitioners (including OECD reviewers and stakeholder organisations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for designing, managing and reviewing regulatory reform in Korea, including institutional roles, procedural requirements (RIA, registry, petitions), and policy principles such as Cost-in/Cost-out and negative-list approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 1: Restraining from newly establishing economic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraining from newly establishing economic regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of seven core principles underpinning the Park administration's regulatory reform approach (Box 2.1). Principle provides normative direction to avoid creating new economic regulations unless necessary; implemented alongside other principles and instruments (e.g., negative-list approach, CICO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 2: Alleviating regulatory cost burdens (Cost-in, Cost-out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleviating regulatory cost burdens (Cost-in, Cost-out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is implemented via the Cost-in, Cost-out (CICO) system to restrict increases in regulatory costs and to induce offsetting reductions; discussed at length including CICO’s banking function, technical support (KDI, KIPA) and coverage over central agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 3: Adopting a negative-list approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting a negative-list approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the seven principles; signals preference for listing prohibited/regulated activities rather than broadly listing allowed activities. Encourages deregulatory orientation by default and is a stated legal/policy objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 4: Enforcing systematic improvement of existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcing systematic improvement of existing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for systematic review and improvement programs (e.g., Regulatory Guillotine, comprehensive plans, RIA) to upgrade regulatory quality rather than ad hoc changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 5: Pursuing prompt improvement of unreasonable local government regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing prompt improvement of unreasonable local government regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises targeted action at subnational level: task forces in local governments, incentive systems for local officials, and publication/competition via the National Regulatory Map to motivate improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 6: Exempting the liability of public officials who proactively carry out regulatory reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempting the liability of public officials who proactively carry out regulatory reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy safeguard to encourage officials to engage in reform without fear of personal liability; implemented to lower administrative risk for proactive improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven principles of regulatory reform – Principle 7: Providing generous incentives to induce active regulatory reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing generous incentives to induce active regulatory reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of incentives (financial, reputational, performance measurement) to motivate central and local agencies to pursue regulatory improvement; linked to performance publication and competition among local governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-in, Cost-out (CICO) system
rubrics_metrics.description: CICO enforces agencies to restrict increases in costs from new or reinforced regulations by abolishing/relaxing regulations that carry equal or greater costs, with a banking function to track total reduced or increased regulatory costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented as pilot (July 2014) and expanded to 27 central agencies; includes a banking function to track reductions/increases; technical review of cost–benefit analyses by regulatory research centres (KDI, KIPA) and a Technical Committee on Regulatory Cost under the RRC. Under CICO, cost–benefit analysis is limited to direct costs and benefits for profit-seeking activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Reform Sinmungo petition process (public petitions handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-stop petition system that integrates existing regulatory petition channels; when a petition is filed, the official must respond within 14 days; if rejected and deemed reasonable by the RRO, the responsible agency must justify the refusal within 3 months; RRC can issue recommendations if refusal rationale is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to increase access and transparency; statistics cited (≈40% petitions accepted as of Nov 2016). The system’s three-step procedure (accept/reject response in 14 days; justification within 3 months upon RRO review; RRC recommendation possible) is a process standard for citizen engagement and petition redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Information Portal and disclosure practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Online portal (http://better.go.kr and mobile site) providing regulatory proposals, the regulatory revision process, and making RIAS public during advance notice of proposed legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portal increases transparency and enables public comment; government avoids collecting personal data to encourage participation; disclosure of RIAS has motivated agencies to improve RIA quality. English portal (e.better.go.kr) and i-Ombudsman extend access to foreigners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) purpose and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: RIA aims to predict and analyse the economic, social and administrative impact of a regulation through objective and scientific means, establishing a standard to determine appropriateness of regulation (Article 2, Framework Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA is a core tool of regulatory quality management; RIAS are published to solicit public comments. Under CICO some CBAs are narrowly scoped to direct costs/benefits for profit-seeking activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment Committee on Emerging Industry standards and tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee of civilian experts reviews regulations related to emerging industries: review public suggestions; abolish regulations unless a rationale exists to retain them; ensure a minimum level of regulation in accordance with international standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to remove unnecessary obstacles to emerging industries (drones, IoT, smart cars, bio-medicine, 3D printing, big data, clouds, O2O). Public safety and health regulations are exempted. Committee statistics: reviewed 271 petitions since March 2016, resolved 94%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-Private Joint Regulation Advancement Initiative (PPJRAI) functions and process
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint initiative (government + non-government) to identify and improve 'thorn-under-the-fingernail' regulations through stakeholder meetings, on-site visits, selection of high-impact regulations and economic-impact analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisationally composed of planning, regulatory improvement, investment environment, and SMEs support divisions with equal public/private representation (13 public officials, 13 non-government reps). Process: identify challenges via business communication; initiate dialogue with relevant agency; jointly improve regulations. Since Sep 2013: ~73 onsite visits, 4,165 regulations identified, 1,532 improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Reform Committee (RRC) mandated functions
rubrics_metrics.description: RRC is mandated to coordinate and deliberate on: basic direction-setting and R&D of regulatory system; review of regulations to be established or reinforced; review of existing regulations and establishment/implementation of comprehensive reform plans; registration and announcement of regulations; stakeholder engagement; inspection and evaluation of reform efforts; and other issues flagged by the chair (Article 24, Framework Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RRC is the final decision-making body at the centre of government (chaired by Prime Minister), divided into Economic and Administrative & Social Sub-Committees; meets twice monthly and reviews approx. 80 proposals (mostly online) with ~8 significant proposals in bi-weekly in-person meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory registry system standards and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: All regulations defined by the Framework Act are subject to registration. Since 2015 a single regulatory provision (the smallest statutory unit) is defined as the unit of registration; the registry is linked to the National Law Information Centre to reflect legislative changes promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration steps: central agency enacts/amends law → reviews provisions and requests RRO approval to update registry → RRO reviews and approves → registration completed. RRC can recommend agencies register omitted regulations. The redefinition of unit and linkage to the law centre aim to ensure objectivity, consistency and public access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive Plan for Regulatory Reform (annual planning and targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: RRC selects focus fields and provides guidelines for agencies to draft regulatory reform plans; agencies submit plans to RRC which compiles a Comprehensive Plan for Regulatory Reform annually and publishes it (by end of February).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to set concrete reduction/improvement goals (example: 2014 goal to reduce economic regulations by 10%, achieving improvement of 995 out of 9,876 regulations = 10.1%). The Framework Act (Article 20) is the legal basis for this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Reform Office (RRO) roles and escalation process
rubrics_metrics.description: RRO (secretariat under Prime Minister’s Office) mediates and coordinates among central agencies on regulatory direction, content and degree; supports the RRC; organises on-site meetings chaired by the Prime Minister; and escalates unresolved conflicts to Ministerial Meetings on Regulatory Reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal basis: Government Organisation Act and Framework Act. RRO also supports petition handling (Sinmungo) and coordinates with technical committees; organises visits to localities to address local regulatory challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative (National Assembly) oversight limitation – RIA on parliamentary bills
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no mandatory regulatory impact assessment (RIA) on parliamentary bills and the RRC lacks control over the legislature; amendments to mandate RIA were proposed but not enacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of mandatory RIA for laws initiated by the National Assembly is identified as a weakness in Korea's regulatory oversight architecture; legislative public hearings and research services exist but no separate institutional reviewer within legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial oversight standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can overturn regulatory decisions deemed illegitimate or unfair; judicial review can remove legal effect of a regulation on substantive as well as procedural grounds; constitutional challenges may be brought to the Constitutional Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review acts as a backstop for regulatory legitimacy; overturning is not restricted to procedural defects but may be substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider international/OECD standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative agencies are encouraged/required to examine international cases and OECD country standards when introducing or reinforcing regulations to detect 'Galapagos Island' (Korea-only) regulations and to check for excessive or insufficient regulation—especially for public safety and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a comparative benchmark requirement to align domestic regulation with international norms; the Investment Committee also uses international standards as a minimum benchmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement and foreign stakeholder access standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder engagement channels include portals (Korean and English), ability for users to submit comments as public or confidential, and option to share company/contact info with competent authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portals (better.go.kr, e.better.go.kr, i-Ombudsman) increase transparency and accessibility for domestic and foreign stakeholders; non-collection of personal info on some channels is used to encourage participation; comments are conveyed to relevant authorities for consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME-targeted regulatory assessment and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailored regulatory approach for SMEs based on SMEs impact assessment (guideline established May 2013) to reduce burdens on small and medium enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SME impact assessments inform differentiated regulatory treatment; Task Forces and SME-support divisions within PPJRAI and other bodies assist in identifying and reforming regulations that disproportionately burden SMEs.
